verses.text: Now Jacob lived in the land where his father had resided, the land of Canaan.

This is the account of Jacob. When Joseph was seventeen years old, he was tending the flock with his brothers, the sons of his father's wives Bilhah and Zilpah, and he brought their father a bad report about them.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.
Then Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more.
He said to them, "Listen to this dream I had:
We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine."
"Do you intend to reign over us?" his brothers asked. "Will you actually rule us?" So they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements.
Then Joseph had another dream and told it to his brothers. "Look," he said, "I had another dream, and this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."
He told his father and brothers, but his father rebuked him and said, "What is this dream that you have had? Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?"
And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said.
Some time later, Joseph's brothers had gone to pasture their father's flocks near Shechem.
Israel said to him, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flocks at Shechem? Get ready; I am sending you to them." "I am ready," Joseph replied.
Then Israel told him, "Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me." So he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. And when Joseph arrived in Shechem,
a man found him wandering in the field and asked, "What are you looking for?"
"I am looking for my brothers," Joseph replied. "Can you please tell me where they are pasturing their flocks?"
"They have moved on from here," the man answered. "I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph set out after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
Now Joseph's brothers saw him in the distance, and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him.
"Here comes that dreamer!" they said to one another.
"Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!"
When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue Joseph from their hands. "Let us not take his life," he said.
"Do not shed his blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him." Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.
So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the robe of many colors he was wearing—
and they took him and threw him into the pit. Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.
And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt.
Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh." And they agreed.
So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes,
returned to his brothers, and said, "The boy is gone! What am I going to do?"
Then they took Joseph's robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood.
They sent the robe of many colors to their father and said, "We found this. Examine it to see whether it is your son's robe or not."
His father recognized it and said, "It is my son's robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!"
Then Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. "No," he said. "I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son." So his father wept for him.
Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 to 50)
context.audience: Israel, the twelve tribes, learning how their fathers came down to Egypt and how God turned evil to good
context.setting: “This is the account of Jacob” (v.2), and it is mostly about Joseph. At seventeen he brings his father a bad report about some of his brothers (v.2). “Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons” and gives him “a robe of many colors,” and his brothers hate him (vv.3-4). Joseph dreams that his brothers’ sheaves bow down to his, and then that “the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me” (vv.5-9). His brothers hate him “even more”; his father rebukes him but “kept in mind what he had said” (vv.8-11). Sent to check on his brothers near Shechem, Joseph finds them at Dothan (vv.12-17). “Here comes that dreamer!” they say, and plot to kill him (vv.18-20). Reuben persuades them to throw him into an empty pit instead, meaning to rescue him (vv.21-24). While they eat, a caravan comes by carrying spices to Egypt, and Judah says, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother?” (vv.25-26). They sell Joseph “for twenty shekels of silver” (v.28). They dip his robe in goat’s blood and send it to Jacob, who says, “Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!” and refuses to be comforted (vv.31-35). In Egypt Joseph is sold to Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh’s guard (v.36).
context.custom: The Hebrew for Joseph’s robe, kethoneth passim, may mean a robe reaching to the hands and feet rather than one of many colors; the same phrase describes the robe of King David’s daughter Tamar (2 Samuel 13:18). Either way it marked him as the favorite, not dressed for work. Caravans carried gum, balm and myrrh from Gilead down the coast road to Egypt. The price, twenty shekels, matches what texts of the early second millennium BC give for a slave, and Leviticus 27:5 values a boy of Joseph’s age at twenty shekels. The traders are called both Ishmaelites and Midianites (vv.25, 28, 36), perhaps because Ishmaelite had become a general name for desert traders (Judges 8:24).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 38 leaves Joseph in Egypt and turns to his brother Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar.
context.timelineBible: Jacob, who once deceived his father with a goat and his brother’s clothes (27:9, 15), is now deceived by his sons with a goat and Joseph’s robe. Stephen tells the story to the Jewish council: “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him” (Acts 7:9). Many Christians see in Joseph a picture of Jesus: loved by his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, and raised up to save them.

translation.meaning: Passim, the word describing Joseph’s robe: perhaps long-sleeved, reaching to the palms and soles, or richly colored. The phrase is used again only of Tamar’s robe (2 Samuel 13:18-19).
A dream. Literally the brothers say, here comes that lord of dreams. Dreams drive Joseph’s whole story, in Canaan, in prison and before Pharaoh.
A pit or cistern dug to catch rainwater. An empty cistern made a prison; Jeremiah was let down into one (Jeremiah 38:6).

gospelParallels.note: The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him; but God was with him.
Judas agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.
He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.

otBackground.note: Jacob deceived Isaac with goats and his brother’s clothes.
He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave.

overview.summary: Joseph, his father’s favorite, dreams that his family will bow to him; his jealous brothers throw him into a pit and sell him to traders, and tell Jacob a wild animal killed him.

history.t: Spices and gums from Gilead were sold in Egypt.
A price for a slave in the early second millennium BC.

customs.t: A favorite son’s robe set him apart from his brothers.
Pits cut in rock to store rainwater.

archaeology.t: A large mound on the route from the hills to the coast road.
Old Babylonian texts give about twenty shekels for a slave.

overview.discussion: Jealousy turned brothers into the sellers of their own brother (vv.4, 11, 28). Is there someone whose favor or success I resent, and what is it doing to me?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: Loves Joseph best and mourns him
One tries to save him; one sells him
